question: “What are we trying to get across with this poster?” What is the designer asking about?
choices: The message people should take from it.
The places where people will see it.
The number of people it should reach.
The date people need to see it by.
note: To “get something across” is to communicate it clearly. “Who are we trying to reach?” asks about the audience.

question: You have six photos for one advert. “Let’s narrow it down,” says the editor. What does she suggest?
choices: Keeping fewer photos under consideration.
Making each photo smaller on the page.
Cropping the sides of the widest photo.
Taking more photos in a similar style.
note: To “narrow it down” is to reduce the number of possibilities. “Crop it” would change a single image.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: A shoe company says, “Our advert needs to stand out.” What do they want people to do?
choices: Notice it among the other adverts.
Recognise the person wearing the shoes.
Remember what the last advert looked like.
Read every word of the description.
note: Something that “stands out” catches your attention. Recognising a familiar person might help an advert do that.

question: “That photo might put people off ordering the curry.” What does the café owner think?
choices: The photo may make the dish less appealing.
The photo may make customers order it later.
The photo may make people expect a bigger portion.
The photo may make people ask how it’s cooked.
note: Here “put people off” means discourage them. “Put off ordering” would mean delay placing an order.

picture.alt: A plate of curry and rice.

question: “The theatre manager is on board with our campaign.” Which statement follows from that?
choices: She supports the idea.
She came up with the idea.
She has paid for the campaign.
She’ll appear in the advert herself.
note: Being “on board” means supporting a plan. Funding it would be one possible way to show support.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: You’re advertising a cycling class for adults who’ve never ridden. The poster says “Beat your personal best!” What do you say at the design meeting?
choices: What about “Your first ride starts here”? Beginners may not have a best time yet.
Can we print the slogan in larger letters so people can see it from the road?
I’d keep that line and use a picture of a rider winning a close race.
Could we add our fastest rider’s time so people know what to aim for?
note: “Your first ride” speaks to the intended audience. “Beat your personal best” suits riders who already track their times.

picture.alt: A bicycle and a pink cycling jersey.

question: Your café client likes the line “Everyone’s favourite coffee”. You surveyed twelve regulars. The client asks whether the claim is fair. What do you say?
choices: Our regulars loved it. I’d quote one of them and say who’s speaking.
The customers we asked all agreed, so I’d leave “everyone” as it is.
Let’s print the word “favourite” larger and make the rest less prominent.
We could ask the same twelve customers again before the posters go up.
note: A named customer’s opinion reflects the evidence you have. Asking the same regulars again would still leave out everyone else.

question: The record shop can afford one advert. Your partner proposes a student newsletter. Before agreeing, you want to know whether it reaches local record buyers. What do you ask?
choices: Do we know how many of its readers buy records around here?
Do they charge more for a full page or for the front cover?
Who else has already booked a space in the next issue?
How soon would the editor need the finished artwork from us?
note: The readership question tests whether the audience fits. “How soon” helps with scheduling once you’ve chosen the newsletter.

question: A client watches your trailer and says, “It feels a bit much.” You can change either the music or the fast cuts today. What do you ask first?
choices: Was it the loud music, the pace of the cuts, or a bit of both?
Would you like us to show the full version at the next meeting?
Should I tell the composer we’re going back to the original track?
Would the same trailer work better at the end of the campaign?
note: Your question turns vague feedback into a choice the client can make. Calling the composer would make sense once the client had named the music.

picture.alt: A clapperboard beside a film reel.

question: The librarian gives you one sentence to pitch your campaign for a book swap. Students keep saying they have nothing new to read. What do you say?
choices: Bring a book you’ve finished and go home with someone else’s favourite.
We’ve prepared three poster designs and a timetable for putting them up.
We’d love to help the library organise more activities for students this year.
The event takes place in the library, where the bookshelves are easy to find.
note: The swap offers those students a specific benefit. The poster timetable belongs in a conversation about how to run the campaign.

picture.alt: An open storybook with a little castle rising from its pages.

question: Your group prefers the red mug advert. The client prefers blue. You have a day and can show both to customers. How do you move things forward?
choices: Let’s show both versions without labels and see which one people remember.
You’re paying, so let’s use blue and save the other version for ourselves.
We all picked red, so could you give us another chance to explain it?
How about putting the red mug on one side and the blue mug on the other?
note: An audience test gives both sides new evidence. “You’re paying” settles who decides without settling which version works.

question: A student has agreed to appear in a campus exhibition. Your partner wants to use her portrait on paid adverts too. Nobody mentioned adverts to her. What do you say?
choices: Let’s ask her about the adverts before we send the photo to print.
We can credit her under the picture and send her a copy afterwards.
Could we crop out the university logo so the advert feels less formal?
She liked the exhibition print, so let’s use exactly that version again.
note: Agreeing to one use leaves the other open. Offering a credit makes sense after she has agreed to the advert.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: Your sports club poster has attracted attention, but students keep asking how to join. There’s space for one more line. What do you suggest?
choices: Let’s add the sign-up address and say when registration closes.
Why don’t we mention the trophies the club won last season?
Could we give the club colours a little more space at the bottom?
What if we put another team photo underneath the first one?
note: An address and a deadline tell interested people what to do next. The trophies might persuade someone who was still deciding.

question: The restaurant owner wants a lunch offer in an evening newsletter. The offer expires at two that same afternoon. How do you raise the problem?
choices: By the time readers see it, lunch will be over. Could we advertise tomorrow’s offer?
Would you like a second mention in the newsletter later that evening?
We can put the expiry time in bold so nobody misses the deadline.
I’ll ask whether they can send us the number of readers after it goes out.
note: Tomorrow’s offer gives readers time to act. Putting today’s deadline in bold would help only if the message arrived before two.

picture.alt: A cooking pot and wooden spoon.

question: The client says, “I like the sketch. I still need to show it to my partners.” Your colleague asks if you can book the printers. What do you say?
choices: She likes the idea, but let’s wait for her partners before we book.
We’ve got her approval. I’ll book the printers for the end of the week.
Could we book a printing slot now so she doesn’t have to wait later?
Shall we send her a finished sample before she meets her partners?
note: Liking a sketch is encouraging. “We’ve got her approval” would fit a clear instruction to go ahead.
